request:
A world in the ALTERNATE-EARTHS-GALLERY sector, kept after Dick; Roth; Turtledove.

The operations this world is built from:

- Historical Rewrite: a universe where changing the past replaces the present (time and causality, inversion).

When we arrive: Thousands of Earths preserve the consequences of different wars, inventions, and accidents.

sourceText: On night 23, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the ALTERNATE-EARTHS-GALLERY sector. Thousands of Earths preserve the consequences of different wars, inventions, and accidents. The memorial bore the name of Dick; Roth; Turtledove precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Aster could follow many histories at once. That very capacity made the lesson difficult: for her, an alternative was almost an object; for the inhabitants of worlds, it was what had not happened. Kesh built his classifications as instruments of falsification: a good category had to state what it did not cover, not merely what it could absorb. At the center of the conflict was Iri, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ 131 they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: Orin feels lives that exist in only one branch and begins to experience every choice as a cemetery of alternatives. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Br — Branching Time: choices produce multiple histories; Tr — Historical Rewrite: changing the past replaces the present. Course references included many-worlds fiction; alternate-timeline fiction. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Kesh answered without raising their voice: ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 132 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Marae persuades him to accept a body capable of perceiving only one history: limitation becomes medicine. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the COUPLING operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — makes previously independent domains determine one another — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a 133 world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. In the hall between sectors, Aster’s Hunger returned. None of the children tried to soothe it. They had begun to believe that some pains should not immediately be turned into demands upon the people nearby. 134 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
